rewear.articles.title: Four ways to wear a pleated midi
rewear.articles.author: Sekar Ayu
rewear.articles.excerpt: One skirt, four different afternoons. Notes on proportion, shoes and what to leave out.

body.text: A pleated midi skirt does a lot of work by itself, so the rest of the outfit can stay quiet. These are four combinations that have held up for us.
With a plain knit and flat shoes
A fitted cardigan or jumper tucked in, and loafers or low boots. The skirt supplies the movement and nothing else needs to.
With a structured jacket
Keep the jacket cropped or boxy so the skirt’s length is still visible. Wool on wool works as long as the tones are close.
With a camp shirt, untucked
Loose on top, pleated below. Leave the top button open and roll the sleeves once.
With nothing extra
A white tee, bare ankles and a good bag. The easiest option, and often the best one.

rewear.articles.title: A closet in Bandung
rewear.articles.author: Raka Pratama
rewear.articles.excerpt: Dara Wibowo has sold secondhand clothes for six years, mostly from a spare room. She talks about sourcing, flaws and what makes a listing honest.

body.text: Dara Wibowo’s spare room has a rail along one wall, a steamer in the corner and a shelf of folded knits sorted by colour. She has sold secondhand clothes from here for six years. This is a profile of how she works, written from a visit and a long conversation.
Finding the pieces

Most of what she lists comes from family clear-outs and weekend markets. She buys slowly and says no often. If she would not wear it herself, or cannot say something true about it, it does not go on the rail.
Writing an honest listing

Flaws go in the first line, not the last. A small moth hole, a replaced zip or a faded armpit is photographed and described. She says it saves her time in the end, because the people who buy are the ones who wanted that piece anyway.
If a buyer is surprised when the parcel opens, I have written the listing badly.
She submits her pieces to RE:WEAR for curator review before they go live, and treats the notes she gets back as free coaching. Her most common fix, she admits, is better light.

rewear.articles.title: How to wash what you thrift
rewear.articles.author: Sekar Ayu
rewear.articles.excerpt: Wool, denim and old cotton each need a different hand. A short guide to cleaning preloved clothes without undoing their age.

body.text: A preloved piece has already survived years of washing. The goal is to keep it going, not to make it look new. A few habits do most of the work.
Wool and knits

Wash by hand in cool water with a small amount of gentle detergent, and press the water out rather than wringing. Dry flat on a towel, away from direct sun. Hanging a wet knit stretches the shoulders for good.
Denim
Wash it less than you think you should. When it does need it, turn it inside out, use cold water and let it dry in the shade. Heat is what shrinks the legs and cooks the colour.
Old cotton and rayon

Test a hidden seam for colour first. Old dyes can run, and rayon weakens when wet, so handle it gently and never twist it. If a smell lingers, an hour in the open air often does more than another wash.

rewear.articles.title: The 90s denim jacket, one more time
rewear.articles.author: Raka Pratama
rewear.articles.excerpt: Boxy, faded and a little too big. Why the chore jacket keeps coming back, and how to tell a good one from a tired one.

body.text: Every few years someone declares the denim jacket finished, and every few years it is back on the rack, a little more faded than before. The version people want now is the boxy chore cut from the nineties: wide through the shoulder, short in the body, with pockets deep enough to be useful.
What a good one feels like
Fabric first. Old denim was woven tighter and heavier, so it softens without going thin. Run a thumb along the elbows and the cuffs. If the cloth feels papery there, it has had its life.

Then the hardware. Original buttons that sit flat, a placket that closes without pulling, and a lining of fading that follows the way the person actually moved. That kind of wear cannot be faked, and it is why preloved denim photographs better than new.
The best denim jackets have an opinion about how they should be worn.
Size up if you want the early-nineties shape. A medium chore jacket sits comfortably over a knit, and a large starts to read as a coat.

rewear.articles.title: How to read a vintage label
rewear.articles.author: Anindya Rahma
rewear.articles.excerpt: A small woven tag can tell you the era, the maker and whether a piece has been altered. Here is what to look for before you buy.

body.text: Before you look at the price, turn the garment inside out. The label is the most honest record a piece carries, and most of what it says is easy to read once you know where to look.
Start with the fibre line

Sewn-in care instructions became standard through the 1970s and 80s, so a piece with none at all is often older, or was made by a very small maker. A short fibre line and nothing else is a good sign. A long list of washing symbols usually points to something newer.
Fibre names are worth reading too. Blends of acetate, rayon and nylon turn up often in older dresses and blouses, while heavy pure wool and cotton drill are common in workwear and tailoring.
Look at how the label is attached

A woven label stitched down on all four sides tends to be older than a printed one or a tag held at the top edge only. The sizing system and the country of origin add more clues, but treat each one as a hint rather than proof.
A label gives you a range, not a date. Two clues that agree are worth more than one that sounds certain.
Check the zip and the stitching

Metal zips with a maker’s name on the pull are common on older pieces, and plastic coil zips arrive later in most categories. Even stitching and finished seams on the inside suggest a garment made to last, which is also what our curators look for.
Every piece on RE:WEAR is photographed with its label wherever it has one. It is the second photo you see when you hover over a product.
